# Ambaṭṭha Sutta (DN 3 (PTS DN i 87))

**ID:** DN 3 (PTS DN i 87)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Ambaṭṭha Sutta
**PTS:** DN i 87
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0101m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3) recounts an encounter in which the arrogant young brahmin student Ambaṭṭha disparages the Buddha's clan (the Sakyas), but is systematically questioned and humbled. In defending the pedigree of the Sakyas against Ambaṭṭha's slurs, the Buddha recounts their ancestral foundation myth: the banished sons of King Okkāka (Sanskrit Ikṣvāku) retreated to the slopes of the Himalayas and cohabited (*saṃvāsa*) with their own sisters out of concern to maintain caste purity [Silk 2009]. During their debate, when Ambaṭṭha hesitates to answer a probing genealogical question, the yakkha Vajrapāṇi appears in the sky holding a blazing iron hammer (*ayokūṭa*), threatening to shatter his head into seven pieces if he does not speak the truth [Gergely]. The text also discusses the thirty-two bodily marks of a great man (*mahāpurisa*), noting that Ambaṭṭha required the Buddha to manifest supernatural powers in order to inspect the two concealed bodily marks [Kingsbury 2002; Nakamura 1999].

Scholars have observed that DN 3, together with DN 4 (*Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta*) and DN 5 (*Kūṭadanta Sutta*), forms a tightly knit stylistic and thematic cluster that presupposes the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) and reflects a relatively developed stage of literary composition [Kingsbury 2002]. Buddhaghosa's commentary (*Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*) elaborates on the narrative, explaining the rationale behind the Sakyan sibling unions in light of caste suitability [Silk 2009].

The sutta possesses an extensive parallel tradition across Indian and non-Indian Buddhist corpora. Curated parallels include a discourse in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 20), an independent early Chinese translation (T 20) datable to before 374 CE that unusually introduces vegetarian monastic precepts [Greene 2016], as well as Tibetan translations in the Kangyur (D 1 and D 6 in the Vinaya) [Levman 2014] and Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta26, SF 43).
